parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor.

markscheme_points.text: charge is on one plate, potential is p.d. betv

hints: Hint 1: Think about the job of a capacitor - it stores electric charge on its two plates. Which charge do we count, and what causes that charge to be there?
Hint 2: Capacitance tells you how much charge is stored for each volt applied. How would you phrase this as charge per unit p.d., being careful where the charge sits and where the p.d. is measured?
parts.proper_answer: Capacitance $C = Q/V$, where $Q$ is the magnitude of charge stored on one plate and $V$ is the potential difference between the plates.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What capacitance measures**
Think of capacitance as storage ability. A bigger capacitor can hold more charge for the same push from the battery. So we define it as charge stored per unit potential difference: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$

Step 2: **Be precise about Q and V**
The two plates hold equal and opposite charges, $+Q$ and $-Q$. We take $Q$ to mean the magnitude of charge on just one plate. $V$ is not the potential of one plate alone, it is the p.d. between the two plates. So capacitance is the charge on one plate per unit p.d. between the plates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
When the two-way switch is in position A, the capacitor is charged so that the potential difference across it is $V$. The switch moves to position B and the capacitor fully discharges through the sensitive ammeter.

The switch moves repeatedly between A and B so that the capacitor charges and then discharges with frequency $f$.
parts.text:
A capacitor of capacitance $C$ is connected into the circuit shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
Show that the average current $I$ in the ammeter is given by the expression

$$I = fCV.$$

markscheme_points.text: charge = CV and time = 1 / f leading to I = f

hints: Hint 1: Start from what the ammeter actually sees. Each time the capacitor discharges, a packet of charge flows through it. How is average current linked to charge and time?
Hint 2: Now link that packet of charge to $C$ and $V$, and link the time for one charge-discharge cycle to the frequency $f$. Combine the two relations.
parts.proper_answer: Charge per discharge $Q = CV$. Time for one cycle $T = 1/f$. Average current $I = Q/T = CV/(1/f) = fCV$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Current is charge per unit time**
Each discharge sends the full stored charge through the ammeter. For one cycle: $$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$ where $Q$ is the charge that flows in time $t$.

Step 2: **Put in Q and t for this circuit**
From capacitance, the charge stored when charged to $V$ is: $$Q = CV$$ The switch charges then discharges with frequency $f$, so one full cycle takes one period: $$t = T = \frac{1}{f}$$ Substitute into $I = Q/t$: $$I = \frac{CV}{1/f} = fCV$$ This is the average current because the flow is in pulses but the meter averages over many cycles.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
For a potential difference $V$ of $150\text{ V}$ and a frequency $f$ of $60\text{ Hz}$, the average current in the ammeter is $4.8\ \mu\text{A}$.

Calculate the capacitance, in pF, of the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: You have $I$, $f$ and $V$ and need $C$. Think about how to rearrange the result from (i) to make $C$ the subject before you put numbers in.
Hint 2: Check your units carefully - $I$ is in microamperes. Convert to amperes first, calculate $C$ in farads, then convert to picofarads using $1\text{ pF} = 10^{-12}\text{ F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Rearrange for C**
From (i): $$I = fCV$$ So: $$C = \frac{I}{fV}$$

Step 2: **Substitute and convert**
$$I = 4.8\,\mu\text{A} = 4.8 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A}$$ $$C = \frac{4.8 \times 10^{-6}}{60 \times 150} = 5.3 \times 10^{-10}\text{ F}$$ Since $1\text{ pF} = 10^{-12}\text{ F}$: $$C = \frac{5.3 \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-12}} \approx 530\text{ pF}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A second capacitor, having the same capacitance as the capacitor in **(b)**, is connected into the circuit of Fig. 7.1. The two capacitors are connected in series.

State and explain the new reading on the ammeter.

markscheme_points.text: or since f and V are constant, current is propo

hints: Hint 1: Recall the rule for two identical capacitors in series. How does the combined capacitance compare to one alone?
Hint 2: If $f$ and $V$ are unchanged, look at $I = f C_{total} V$. How must the charge transferred per cycle and hence the average current change when $C_{total}$ changes?
Hint 3: Use the halving idea to work out the new ammeter value from the old $4.8\,\mu\text{A}$ reading.
parts.proper_answer: For two equal $C$ in series, $1/C_{total} = 1/C + 1/C$, so $C_{total} = C/2$. Charge per cycle $Q = C_{total}V$ is halved, so with same $f$ and $V$, $I = fC_{total}V$ is halved. New reading $= 2.4\,\mu\text{A}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **New total capacitance**
For series: $$\frac{1}{C_{total}} = \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{C} = \frac{2}{C}$$ So: $$C_{total} = \frac{C}{2}$$ The pair acts like a capacitor half as big.

Step 2: **Effect on charge per cycle**
Charged to the same $V$, the charge that can be stored and then discharged each time is: $$Q = C_{total}V = \frac{CV}{2}$$ So only half the charge flows through the ammeter per discharge.

Step 3: **Effect on average current**
Since $f$ and $V$ are constant, $I = fC_{total}V$ is directly proportional to $C_{total}$. Halving $C_{total}$ halves $I$: $$I_{new} = \frac{4.8}{2} = 2.4\,\mu\text{A}$$
